analysis.one_liner: Lets states tax employer health plans to fund universal coverage and care for the medically uninsurable.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to let states fund health coverage for the uninsured never got a committee vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law (ERISA) currently bars states from taxing or regulating most employer health plans, including plans large employers run themselves. This bill would carve out an exception: states could apply to tax all health plans equally, force them into state risk pools for people no insurer will cover, set hospital payment rates, and fund plans to expand coverage. The bill went to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: State governments, which gain the power to finance universal health plans and risk pools; and the millions of uninsured and medically uninsurable residents those programs would cover. Today, ERISA's preemption means self-insured employer plans pay nothing toward state health financing, so the burden of caring for the uninsured falls on everyone else.

how_it_helps.text: Lets states, upon federal approval, impose a uniform tax or surcharge on all health plans doing business in the state — including self-insured employer plans currently exempt under ERISA — and use the money for a risk pool for the medically uninsurable or to expand access to care [S3]
Forbids states from giving tax breaks to some plan types or sizes, so large self-insured employers could not shift the cost onto smaller plans [S3]

Allows states to set hospital payment rates prospectively and include charges for uncompensated care such as indigent care and bad debts, instead of leaving hospitals to shift those costs informally onto other patients [S3]
Requires the Health and Human Services Department to verify each state plan has sufficient resources and capacity, and to report publicly on the results of the first approved plans [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large employers that self-insure their workers' health plans, and health insurers, who would for the first time pay state health taxes or risk-pool assessments set at the same rate for every plan. Those costs could be passed to employers' benefit budgets; hospitals and providers would face state-set payment rates.

drawbacks.text: New state taxes on employer health plans would raise the cost of providing benefits, a cost that could fall on workers through reduced wages or benefits [S3]
Federal approval only checks that a state plan has resources and capacity; it does not guarantee a state's program actually covers the uninsured, and results would vary state by state [S3]
Allowing state-by-state hospital rate-setting and taxes would replace one national rule with up to 50 different systems, adding administrative complexity for multi-state employers and providers [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is an enabling measure, not a program itself: it removes a federal legal barrier and lets states experiment with financing universal coverage, with a uniform-tax safeguard to prevent large employers from dodging the cost. The trade-off is real — employer plans and insurers would pay new state taxes, and outcomes would depend on what each state does — but the safeguard design and the federal capacity review address the most obvious objection.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in September 1992 with bipartisan support, it was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never marked it up or voted on it before Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Dave Durenberger introduced the bill on September 10, 1992, joined by Senators Bradley, Jeffords, Moynihan, Chafee, and Wellstone — three Republicans and three Democrats [S1][S3]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day it was introduced [S5]
No further action — no committee markup, no floor vote, no House action — was ever recorded before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large self-insured employers and health plans, which kept their ERISA exemption from state health taxes and risk-pool obligations, and continued to leave the cost of uncompensated care with everyone else.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Self-insured employers kept their tax exemption

for.name: Sen. Dave Durenberger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship

for.name: Sens. Bradley, Jeffords, Moynihan, Chafee, and Wellstone

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the four months remaining in the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and five cosponsors split evenly between the parties — three Republicans and three Democrats — and no recorded vote ever showed opposition because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: Under ERISA these plans are exempt from state health taxes and risk-pool requirements; the bill would make them pay the same uniform tax or surcharge as everyone else, ending a structural cost shift onto state programs and other payers.

Insurers would face the same nondiscriminatory state taxes and risk-pool participation as employer plans, but state universal plans funded by those taxes could also compete with or displace private coverage in some states.

States could set hospital payment rates prospectively and add explicit charges for uncompensated care, converting informal cost-shifting into set rates; providers would also be subject to state health taxes.
